identity.title: Saddle (perineal) sensory loss and reduced anal tone

technique.how: With consent and a chaperone, test light touch and pinprick over the perineum, perianal skin, and inner thighs (S2-S5) comparing sides and asking about altered sensation on wiping. Then digital rectal examination assessing resting tone and voluntary squeeze, and the anal wink reflex; check a post-void residual bladder volume at the same time.
technique.prerequisites: Explain the examination, chaperone, privacy; document baseline bladder and bowel function and time of onset.
technique.contraindications: Patient refusal; anal pathology making examination intolerable (perform sensory testing and bladder scan regardless).

interpretation.positive_finding: Reduced perianal/saddle sensation or reduced anal tone in a patient with back pain, bilateral sciatica, or new urinary symptoms is a red flag for cauda equina compression and warrants emergency MRI; pooled red flags are more specific than sensitive.
interpretation.negative_finding: Normal saddle sensation and anal tone do not exclude cauda equina syndrome (pooled red-flag sensitivities only 0.19-0.43); digital rectal examination alone did not discriminate MRI-confirmed CES.
interpretation.pitfalls: Subjective altered sensation is often missed unless asked about wiping; anal tone is unreliable and examiner-dependent. Painless retention with overflow incontinence is the most ominous late sign and is often misattributed to prostatism.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: emergency whole-lumbar MRI and spinal surgery referral, bladder scan/catheter. Negative: do not de-escalate if urinary retention or bilateral leg symptoms are present.

sources.citation: Dionne N, Adefolarin A, Kunzelman D, et al. What is the diagnostic accuracy of red flags related to cauda equina syndrome (CES), when compared to Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)? A systematic review. Musculoskelet Sci Pract. 2019;42:125-133.
Gooding BW, Higgins MA, Calthorpe DA. Does rectal examination have any value in the clinical diagnosis of cauda equina syndrome? Br J Neurosurg. 2013;27(2):156-159.
Bell DA, Collie D, Statham PF. Cauda equina syndrome: what is the correlation between clinical assessment and MRI scanning? Br J Neurosurg. 2007;21(2):201-203.
Domen PM, Hofman PA, van Santbrink H, Weber WE. Predictive value of clinical characteristics in patients with suspected cauda equina syndrome. Eur J Neurol. 2009;16(3):416-419.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Never use a normal rectal examination or normal saddle sensation to withhold emergency MRI when there is new urinary retention, incontinence, or bilateral sciatica.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Suspected cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency; MRI should be obtained within hours because neurological deterioration is unpredictable and often irreversible.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Anal tone assessment is subjective and, in one series of 57 suspected CES, DRE had test accuracy 51% (diagnostic odds ratio 1.42) against MRI; perceived saddle numbness is reported by patients more reliably than it is elicited by pinprick.

extraction_notes: Dionne 2019 (corrected 2019/2021, PMIDs 31300389/33722511) pools saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal tone against MRI in 6 studies (N=569): abstract gives only the range across seven red flags, pooled sensitivity 0.19 (0.09-0.33) to 0.43 (0.30-0.56) and specificity 0.62 (0.59-0.73) to 0.88 (0.85-0.92); the per-finding table is not visible (no PMC full text) so no finding-specific estimate can be entered and evidence_status is not_quantified. Primary studies retrieved (Gooding 2013 DRE accuracy 51%, Bell 2007 'altered perineal sensation' diagnostic accuracy 0.60, Domen 2009) report accuracy or ORs without extractable sens/spec in their abstracts. A verifier with access to Dionne Table 3 should fill the saddle-anaesthesia and anal-tone rows.
